sections.body: This field is the application of machine learning and language models to the routine and judgment-heavy work of accounting and finance. Right now artificial intelligence is reading and extracting data from invoices, contracts, and bank statements, then posting entries or flagging mismatches. It is drafting narrative sections of financial reports, reconciling balances across ledgers, and scanning transactions for patterns that suggest fraud. In tax, it is matching local rules to transaction data to estimate liabilities and prepare filings. In treasury, it is forecasting cash positions from payment history and open invoices. These are working systems, not prototypes, used inside accounting departments and software platforms.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Routine extraction and reconciliation are fairly reliable when documents are clean and formats are consistent, but messy scans, unusual contracts, and multi-entity consolidations still need human review. Forecasting models can produce plausible numbers yet fail when a supply shock or sudden demand shift falls outside training data. Continuous audit and fraud detection reduce manual sampling but generate many false positives, and auditors still own the final judgment. Tax and jurisdictional compliance remain hard because rules change often and models can miss local nuance. Across the 732 AI tools tracked on this site, the most mature are in payables and receivables, while governance and digital asset accounting are thinner. Honest limits include explainability, data quality, and the fact that these systems do not understand accounting concepts, they predict likely outputs from patterns.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from core reporting outward to specialized and control functions. A reader would start with Financial Reporting and Synthesis to see how models draft and assemble statements, then turn to Forecasting and Planning for projections and scenario work. Tax and Jurisdictional Compliance covers the rule-matching and filing side, while Continuous Audit and Assurance and Fraud Detection and Forensics show how the same transaction data is checked for errors and misconduct. Payables and Receivables and Treasury and Liquidity focus on cash movement and working capital, and Sustainability and Carbon Accounting and Digital Asset Accounting cover newer reporting demands. Governance, Risk and Financial Data Security closes the loop by addressing how the models themselves are controlled, audited, and kept from leaking financial data.
